promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is a deflected succession (plagioclimax)?
options: A community held at a stage before the natural climax by human activity such as grazing
The earliest pioneer stage of succession
A succession occurring entirely underwater
A succession that reaches its natural climax community
questions.explain: Continued human or animal interference, such as grazing or mowing, stops succession reaching its natural climax.

questions.q: Activated T-helper cells assist the humoral response chiefly by:
options: Producing large amounts of antibody themselves
Directly killing pathogens with toxins
Releasing cytokines that stimulate B-cells and phagocytes
Engulfing antigen-presenting cells
questions.explain: T-helper cells secrete cytokines (interleukins) that promote clonal expansion of B-cells and increase phagocytic activity.

questions.q: During phagocytosis of a pathogen, the engulfed microbe is destroyed when:
options: Memory cells are produced directly
A phagosome fuses with a lysosome and lysozymes hydrolyse the pathogen
The phagocyte divides by mitosis
Antibodies are released into the cytoplasm
questions.explain: The pathogen is enclosed in a phagosome which fuses with a lysosome; lytic enzymes (lysozymes) then digest it.

questions.q: During the cross-bridge cycle, the binding of ATP to the myosin head causes it to:
options: Release calcium ions
Detach from the actin filament
Bend and perform the power stroke
Bind more tightly to actin
questions.explain: ATP binding to the myosin head breaks the cross-bridge, detaching it from actin so the cycle can repeat.

questions.q: The clonal selection and activation of a specific B-cell typically requires:
options: Only the antigen binding to the B-cell receptor
Antigen binding plus stimulation by an activated T-helper cell releasing cytokines
Phagocytosis of the B-cell
Binding to a memory cell
questions.explain: Most B-cells require both antigen binding and signals (cytokines) from T-helper cells to divide and differentiate.

questions.q: The myoglobin dissociation curve lies to the LEFT of the haemoglobin curve, which means myoglobin:
options: Releases oxygen at higher partial pressures than haemoglobin
Has a higher affinity for oxygen and acts as an oxygen store in muscle
Carries four oxygen molecules like haemoglobin
Cannot bind oxygen at low partial pressures
questions.explain: Myoglobin's high oxygen affinity means it only releases oxygen at very low partial pressures, acting as a reserve store in muscle.

questions.q: During primary succession, what is the key role of the pioneer species?
options: They colonise bare rock and begin soil formation
They are the top predators of the food web
They form the stable climax community
They prevent any further species from establishing
questions.explain: Pioneers such as lichens colonise inhospitable bare surfaces and start building soil for later species.

questions.q: What is the role of decomposers (saprobionts) in the carbon cycle?
options: They break down dead organic matter, releasing CO2 through their respiration
They fix atmospheric carbon dioxide
They build carbon into fossil fuels
They convert nitrate to nitrogen gas
questions.explain: Decomposers respire as they break down dead matter, returning the carbon it contains to the air as CO2.

questions.q: The cells lining the proximal convoluted tubule have many mitochondria and microvilli because they:
options: Produce urine of variable concentration
Secrete ADH into the filtrate
Carry out a large amount of active reabsorption requiring ATP and surface area
Filter the blood under high pressure
questions.explain: Reabsorbing most of the glucose, ions and water demands abundant ATP (mitochondria) and a large absorbing surface (microvilli).

questions.q: Ultrafiltration in the renal glomerulus occurs because:
options: High hydrostatic blood pressure forces small molecules through the basement membrane, which acts as a filter
Plasma proteins are actively secreted into the filtrate
The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, lowering pressure
Active transport pushes plasma into the Bowman's capsule
questions.explain: High pressure (helped by a narrower efferent arteriole) forces water and small solutes through the basement membrane, which holds back proteins and cells.

questions.q: When using random quadrats to estimate the abundance of a species in a large field, why must the quadrats be placed randomly?
options: To ensure quadrats overlap
To avoid bias so the sample fairly represents the whole area
To count every individual present
To save time
questions.explain: Random placement avoids sampling bias, giving an estimate that fairly represents the whole study area.

questions.q: Energy transferred to a trophic level is 50,000 kJ per m2 per yr and that passed on to the next level is 5,000 kJ per m2 per yr. What is the percentage efficiency of transfer?
The basement membrane of the glomerulus prevents which component of blood from entering the filtrate?
options: Plasma proteins such as albumin
Urea
Glucose
Water
questions.explain: The basement membrane acts as a molecular sieve, holding back large plasma proteins and blood cells while small molecules pass through.

questions.q: For the mark-release-recapture method to give a valid estimate, which assumption must hold?
options: All marked individuals are recaptured
Marking does not affect survival and marked individuals mix randomly with the population
The population doubles between samples
Marked individuals reproduce faster
questions.explain: The estimate assumes marks are harmless and that marked individuals redistribute randomly before the second sample.

questions.q: Agglutination by antibodies helps destroy pathogens because:
options: Each antibody has two binding sites, so it clumps pathogens together, making them easier for phagocytes to engulf
It marks the antibody for destruction
It neutralises bacterial toxins by hydrolysis
It directly lyses the bacterial cell wall
questions.explain: With two binding sites an antibody can link several pathogens into clumps that phagocytes engulf more efficiently.

questions.q: For herd immunity to interrupt transmission of a pathogen, the proportion of the population that must be immune depends mainly on:
options: The age of the youngest individual
The colour of the vaccine vial
The cost of the vaccine
How easily the pathogen spreads from person to person
questions.explain: More infectious pathogens require a higher proportion of immune individuals to break chains of transmission and protect the susceptible.

questions.q: Which type of white blood cell is a non-specific phagocyte that engulfs pathogens?
options: T-helper cell
Plasma cell
Neutrophil
B-lymphocyte
questions.explain: Neutrophils are phagocytes that engulf and digest pathogens non-specifically as part of the innate immune response.

questions.q: Antibodies passed from mother to baby in breast milk give the baby:
options: Natural passive immunity
Artificial passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial active immunity
questions.explain: The antibodies are received naturally (via milk/placenta) and the baby does not make them itself, so it is natural passive immunity.

questions.q: Which describes a density-independent factor affecting a population?
options: A severe frost killing organisms regardless of population size
Predation
Competition for nesting sites
Disease spread in a crowded population
questions.explain: A frost affects the same proportion of individuals whatever the density, so it is density-independent.

questions.q: A desert mammal that produces very concentrated urine is likely to have:
options: A very short loop of Henle
A long loop of Henle, allowing a steep medullary solute gradient
A glomerulus that filters very little blood
No collecting ducts
questions.explain: A long loop of Henle generates a stronger medullary concentration gradient, enabling more water reabsorption and highly concentrated urine.

questions.q: At high altitude, where the partial pressure of oxygen is low, the oxygen dissociation curve of a well-adapted animal is often shifted to the LEFT because:
options: A higher oxygen affinity helps haemoglobin load oxygen at the low oxygen partial pressures found there
Haemoglobin must release oxygen more readily to tissues
Carbon dioxide levels are always higher at altitude
Tissues require less oxygen at altitude
questions.explain: A leftward shift (higher affinity) allows haemoglobin to become saturated despite the low oxygen partial pressure of high-altitude air.

questions.q: On a cold day, the body conserves heat by:
options: Increased sweating
Relaxation of erector pili muscles
Vasodilation of skin arterioles
Vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, reducing blood flow to the surface
questions.explain: Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow near the skin surface, decreasing heat loss by radiation.

questions.q: Glucagon raises blood glucose principally by stimulating:
options: Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver
Glycogenesis and glucose uptake
Insulin secretion from beta cells
The conversion of glucose to fat
questions.explain: Glucagon promotes breakdown of glycogen (glycogenolysis) and synthesis of glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (gluconeogenesis) in the liver.

questions.q: HIV cannot replicate without a host cell because it:
options: Lacks the enzymes and ribosomes needed for protein synthesis and energy release
Reproduces only by binary fission
Has a thick cell wall
Is too small to contain genetic material
questions.explain: As a virus, HIV has no metabolic machinery of its own and must use the host cell's enzymes and ribosomes to replicate.

questions.q: Which process in the nitrogen cycle returns nitrogen gas to the atmosphere, reducing soil fertility?
options: Nitrification
Nitrogen fixation
Ammonification
Denitrification
questions.explain: Denitrifying bacteria in anaerobic soils convert nitrate back to nitrogen gas, lowering soil nitrogen.

questions.q: Antigenic variation makes some pathogens (e.g. influenza virus) hard to combat because:
options: They destroy all the host's T-cells
They cannot be engulfed by phagocytes
They reproduce too slowly for memory cells to form
They change their surface antigens, so memory cells from previous infections no longer recognise them
questions.explain: Frequent changes to surface antigens mean existing memory cells are no longer complementary, so a new primary response is needed each time.

questions.q: What is the role of saprobiotic (decomposer) bacteria and fungi in ammonification?
options: They release nitrogen gas from nitrate
They fix atmospheric nitrogen
They oxidise nitrite to nitrate
They convert nitrogen-containing compounds in dead matter into ammonium ions
questions.explain: Decomposers break down proteins and other nitrogen compounds in dead organisms, releasing ammonium ions.

questions.q: Which sampling technique is most appropriate for estimating the population of a non-motile plant such as clover in a field?
options: Pitfall traps
Sweep netting
Mark-release-recapture
Quadrats placed at random
questions.explain: Random quadrats are ideal for sessile organisms like plants, where individuals can be counted in a known area.

questions.q: The ELISA test uses antibodies linked to an enzyme to:
options: Vaccinate a patient against a disease
Destroy a pathogen in a sample
Replace a missing hormone
Detect the presence of a specific antigen or antibody by producing a colour change
questions.explain: In an ELISA, an enzyme-linked antibody binds its target and the enzyme then catalyses a colour change, revealing presence and amount.

questions.q: Phosphocreatine is important in muscle contraction because it:
options: Binds to troponin
Rapidly regenerates ATP from ADP at the start of intense exercise
Forms the cross-bridges with actin
Provides the calcium needed for contraction
questions.explain: Phosphocreatine donates a phosphate to ADP to quickly resynthesise ATP, sustaining contraction during short bursts of activity.
